contextTopics.label: Russlands Krieg gegen die Ukraine
background: Russland überfiel die Ukraine am 24. Februar 2022 in vollem Umfang. Vorausgegangen war die Annexion der Krim im März 2014 und der von Russland unterstützte bewaffnete Konflikt im Donbas ab April 2014.

Die UN-Generalversammlung verurteilte den Angriff am 2. März 2022 mit 141 zu 5 Stimmen und forderte den sofortigen Rückzug. Die EU, die USA und weitere Staaten verhängten seither mehrere Sanktionspakete.
Der Internationale Strafgerichtshof erließ im März 2023 einen Haftbefehl gegen Wladimir Putin wegen der Verschleppung ukrainischer Kinder.
Österreich ist militärisch neutral, beteiligt sich aber an den EU-Sanktionen und leistet humanitäre Hilfe. Waffenlieferungen erfolgen nicht.

contextTopics.label: Krieg in Gaza und im Nahen Osten
background: Die Hamas verübte am 7. Oktober 2023 einen Großangriff auf Israel mit rund 1.200 Toten und etwa 250 Verschleppten. Israel begann daraufhin eine großangelegte Militäroperation im Gazastreifen.
Der Konflikt reicht weit zurück: Israel wurde 1948 gegründet, es folgten mehrere Kriege mit arabischen Nachbarstaaten. Der Gazastreifen wird seit 2007 von der Hamas kontrolliert.
Der Internationale Gerichtshof befasst sich seit Dezember 2023 mit einer Klage Südafrikas wegen mutmaßlichen Völkermords; ein Urteil in der Hauptsache steht aus.

Zahlenangaben zu Opfern stammen je nach Meldung von unterschiedlichen Stellen — der von der Hamas geführten Gesundheitsbehörde, israelischen Angaben oder UN-Organisationen. Sie sind selten unabhängig überprüfbar.

contextTopics.label: Handelskonflikte und Zölle
background: Die USA erhoben ab 2018 unter Präsident Trump Zölle auf Stahl, Aluminium und zahlreiche chinesische Waren. China antwortete mit Gegenzöllen. Teile davon blieben auch unter der Nachfolgeregierung bestehen.
Die EU ist als Zollunion für die Handelspolitik ihrer Mitgliedsstaaten zuständig — Österreich verhandelt also nicht selbst, sondern die Europäische Kommission.
Zölle wirken auf zwei Wegen: Sie verteuern eingeführte Waren für Verbraucher im Einfuhrland und treffen Exporteure im Ausland. Wer die Kosten trägt, ist wirtschaftswissenschaftlich umstritten.

contextTopics.label: Inflation und Zinspolitik der EZB
background: Die Europäische Zentralbank hat als vorrangiges Ziel Preisstabilität, definiert als 2 Prozent Inflation mittelfristig. Sie steuert darüber den Leitzins für den gesamten Euroraum.
Nach Jahren mit Null- und Negativzinsen begann die EZB im Juli 2022 mit Zinserhöhungen, um die stark gestiegene Inflation zu dämpfen — ausgelöst unter anderem durch Energiepreise und Lieferengpässe.

Österreich lag bei der Inflationsrate über Jahre über dem Euroraum-Durchschnitt. Die Gründe dafür sind umstritten; genannt werden unter anderem Energiepreise, Mietanpassungen und der Gastronomiesektor.

contextTopics.label: Klimapolitik und Klimaziele
background: Im Pariser Abkommen von 2015 verpflichteten sich fast alle Staaten, die Erderwärmung deutlich unter 2 Grad gegenüber dem vorindustriellen Niveau zu halten und 1,5 Grad anzustreben.
Die EU hat sich auf Klimaneutralität bis 2050 festgelegt und Zwischenziele für 2030 beschlossen. Österreich strebt Klimaneutralität bis 2040 an — früher als die EU-Vorgabe.

Der Weltklimarat IPCC fasst regelmäßig den Forschungsstand zusammen. Dass die Erwärmung überwiegend menschengemacht ist, gilt dort als gesichert; umstritten sind Tempo, regionale Folgen und Gegenmaßnahmen.

contextTopics.label: Regulierung künstlicher Intelligenz
background: Die Europäische Kommission legte 2021 den Entwurf für den AI Act vor, die weltweit erste umfassende Regulierung künstlicher Intelligenz. Er stuft Anwendungen nach Risiko ein und verbietet einige ganz.
Das Gesetz gilt für Anbieter, die ihre Systeme im EU-Markt anbieten — unabhängig davon, wo sie sitzen. Die Pflichten greifen gestaffelt über mehrere Jahre.
Kritik kommt von zwei Seiten: Teilen der Industrie, die Wettbewerbsnachteile befürchten, und Bürgerrechtsorganisationen, denen die Ausnahmen für Sicherheitsbehörden zu weit gehen.

contextTopics.label: Österreichische Innenpolitik
background: Österreich ist eine parlamentarische Demokratie. Der Nationalrat mit 183 Abgeordneten wird alle fünf Jahre gewählt; die Regierung braucht dessen Vertrauen.
Der Bundespräsident wird direkt gewählt, ernennt die Regierung und kann sie entlassen — eine Befugnis, die historisch selten genutzt wurde.
Untersuchungsausschüsse sind ein Minderheitsrecht: Ein Viertel der Abgeordneten kann einen einsetzen, ohne Zustimmung der Mehrheit.

contextTopics.label: Raiffeisen Bank International
background: Die Raiffeisen Bank International (RBI) ist eine der größten Banken Österreichs mit Schwerpunkt in Zentral- und Osteuropa. Sie ging 2010 aus der Fusion von RZB-Teilen und Raiffeisen International hervor.
Der Raiffeisen-Sektor ist genossenschaftlich aufgebaut: lokale Raiffeisenbanken, darüber Landesbanken, darüber die RBI. Diese Struktur erklärt, warum Entscheidungen oft mehrere Ebenen betreffen.
Das Russland-Geschäft der RBI steht seit dem Angriff auf die Ukraine unter besonderer Beobachtung von EZB und US-Behörden. Ein Rückzug wurde mehrfach angekündigt und verzögerte sich.

items.title: You Don't Need a Transformation. You Need One Repair.
items.summary: Image You don't need a transformation. You need one repair. You've done the big change. Maybe more than once. The reorg, the new framework, the tooling migration, the all-hands where someone put "cultural change" on a slide. Months of disruption, a real budget, everybody's attention. And here you are, hitting the same frictions you started with. The status that stays green until it snaps. The retro that changes nothing. The team that waits more than it works. That isn't bad luck, and it isn't because you picked the wrong framework this time. It's because the unit of change was always too big. A transformation tries to change everything at once, which means it can't isolate what actually moved the needle, can't be inspected while it's happening, and can't be undone when a piece of it makes things worse. You find out if it worked a year later, when it's too late and too expensive to matter. There's a smaller unit that actually moves. One repair at a time. Why the big change keeps missing The gap the transformation is supposed to close is real. In Digital.ai's 2025 State of Agile, somewhere between 55 and 64% of organizations said they had good visibility into their work, while 63% in the same population said they struggled to actually deliver it. More process, more oversight, and the delivery problem is still there. That's the tell: the thing that's weak isn't the framework. It's a behavior underneath it that no rollout installs. So instead of installing another process, you repair the fundamental underneath the friction. Not all eight fundamentals, not the whole team, not this quarter. One friction, one fundamental, one small move you can watch. The loop The whole system runs on four steps. It's small enough to run this week. Spot the Friction Signal. Start from what the team actually feels, the pattern people recognize instantly. Not a complaint, not a diagnosis. "We keep getting surprised." "The real meeting happens in the hallway." Name the weak fundamental. A friction tells you where to look. A few honest questions tell you what you're looking at, the fundamental most likely under pressure. Usually more than one, which is fine. Try one Repair Move. A small, testable change you can run in a few weeks and actually inspect. Not a transformation. One thing. Observe what shifts. Then you watch, honestly. Did anything change? If nothing surfaced, the move didn't take, and that's information too. That's it. Spot, name, try, observe. Then go around again. The part that makes it honest Two things keep this from becoming just another framework. First, a friction almost never has a single cause with a single fix. The loop points you at the fundamental most likely under pressure and hands you a repair to try, not the answer. You run it as an experiment and let what shifts tell you whether you aimed right. Second, the reason a fundamental eroded almost always sits in the system around the team, not in the team's willpower. "Just be more transparent" is useless advice when roughly 6 in 10 employees say they're afraid to speak up at work, as a 2026 Radical Candor survey found. You don't fix that with a poster. You change what surfacing a problem costs, one small move at a time, and you watch whether the truth starts arriving earlier. Small enough to actually do A transformation asks you to bet a year on a change you can't inspect. A repair asks you to bet two weeks on a change you can. If it works, you feel it fast and you keep going. If it doesn't, you've lost a fortnight and learned something specific. That asymmetry is the whole argument. So the next move isn't a program. It's picking the one friction your team feels most, and the fundamental most likely under it. That takes about two minutes to find. Take the two-minute self-diagnostic → https://www.fundamentalsfirst.eu/self-diagnostic Your framework isn't broken. Your fundamentals are. Scrum on!

items.title: Comets may have destroyed life's ingredients instead of delivering them to Earth
items.summary: A century-old theory about the origins of life on Earth may be wrong. New research from the University of Cambridge suggests that comets traveled too fast and struck at unfavorable angles for the fragile molecules needed for life to survive, making successful delivery extraordinarily unlikely. Surprisingly, Mars may have had a better chance of receiving these cosmic ingredients, although even there the odds were slim. The findings point toward asteroids or chemical processes on Earth as more plausible sources of life's building blocks.

After years of investment, the modernization had delivered nothing, millions had gone to consultants, and the company was downsizing. What went wrong? The obvious way This is not a unique story. A lot of companies overcomplicate their modernizations. At this company, they already had a high-performing Scrum Team managing their core product. The obvious move was to engage their existing Product Owner and empower them to lead the modernization effort with the current Scrum Team. They already understood the business, the customers, the edge cases, and the real constraints. They had the empirical knowledge that only comes from delivering value Sprint after Sprint, and they'd just wrapped up a major initiative successfully. Done right, this was a chance to energize the team that already knew the product best. They could have started replacing the existing system a piece at a time and learning as they went. If leadership wanted to move faster, they could have added additional staff and support to the existing Scrum Team. The other way Instead of engaging their existing Scrum Team, the company formed several new Scrum Teams to do the modernization effort. Leadership then decided that because the new Scrum Teams were just rebuilding the current product, they didn't need a Product Owner . They worked for six months without a Product Owner, but nothing usable was delivered. When the organization finally did add Product Owners, they weren't really empowered to make real business decisions. It was too little, too late. Here's what went wrong: Siloed teams . Not only were they separated from the current team, but the new teams were formed around technology silos which created unnecessary dependencies. No empowered Product Owner . No one was empowered to steer the modernization effort. Big-bang thinking . Unrealistic, leadership-defined deadlines, no incremental delivery. Ignoring the people closest to the work. Money and Vice Presidents instead of engaging the team that already knew the product. No Empirical approach. They didn't adjust their delivery approach beyond just surface-level changes when things weren't going well. Development and testing were in separate Sprints. They hired a design firm who put together a front-end design and html in one Sprint, and then back-end development and testing was done in the following Sprint. Repeatedly what was delivered couldn't be used and had to be sent back which caused delays on top of delays. I have watched versions of this story play out before, and throwing more money at it is not the answer and siloed teams rarely work well. The result of getting the structure wrong Ignoring existing institutional knowledge and starting over with a group that had no empowered Product Owner was not “saving money.” It was the most expensive decision they could have made. In the end, the company wasted so much money that it led to downsizing. They never got their modernization. Instead, they got restructured. How to get it right Great modernization efforts don't happen by accident. They start with the right structure and the right people already in place. Start with good structure First off, a Product Owner is not optional. A Product Owner owns the Product Goal, orders the backlog, and makes strategic decisions. Without an empowered Product Owner, a Scrum Team is just a group of people throwing code around. Energize your high-performing teams Leadership should not redesign the org chart every time they get excited about a new technology. Leadership should remove impediments, make sure the team has the resources they need, and make sure the team is working together effectively. Keep the high-performing teams. Give them the support they need. If the old system truly needs to be replaced, the people who already understand the volume, the data, and the business rules are the ones best positioned to make that transition safely and incrementally. Plan for Incremental Delivery A year of work with nothing usable to show for it is not Agile. Modernization doesn't have to mean a big-bang rewrite. Encourage the Scrum Team to break the work down. They should deliver small, usable pieces of the new system, get feedback, and build on it. Let the team plan their own Sprints instead of chasing top-down deadlines set before anyone understood the scope of the work. Three questions to ask before you modernize If your organization is about to launch a modernization effort, ask yourself three questions. Who has organizational knowledge - Who already owns the current Product and has the deepest knowledge of it? Is the team structured for success? - Are we organizing around the Product or around technology silos? Can we allow them to self-organize? Are we planning for incremental delivery? - Will we deliver usable increments every Sprint, or are we planning a multi-year rewrite…

items.title: The Product Goal Nobody Uses
items.summary: Image In Professional Scrum Product Owner training, I ask every class the same question on the second day: describe your Product Goal. Almost everyone can answer. Most have one written down somewhere, on a slide or in a Confluence page, and the room moves on quickly. Then I ask a second question: which items in your current backlog would you remove because they do not contribute to that goal? That question takes longer. The 2020 Scrum Guide added the Product Goal as the commitment for the Product Backlog [1]. Before that revision, teams were expected to have a product direction, but Scrum never formalized it or tied it to the backlog. The 2020 update made the goal a first-class artifact commitment, alongside the Sprint Goal and the Definition of Done. The Scrum Guide describes the rest of the backlog as emerging "to define what will fulfill the Product Goal" [1]. The backlog is supposed to grow from the goal. Most teams fill the backlog first and write the goal second. The Backlog-First Problem Teams with an existing backlog and a new Product Goal write a goal that fits what they already have. They have no real choice: the backlog contains years of stakeholder requests, technical debt, customer feedback, and executive priorities. Any goal specific enough to exclude some of those would immediately surface conflicts nobody has resolved. So the goal ends up broad enough to cover everything, because it was shaped to match. Stefan Wolpers calls this "retroactively squeezed under a made-up Product Goal" and names it cargo-cult Scrum [2]. The practices are present, but the logic that gives them meaning is gone. Writing the goal to fit the backlog reverses the relationship the Guide describes: the backlog is supposed to flow from the goal, not precede it. When a new request arrives, the question should be: does this advance toward the Product Goal? Teams with a retroactive goal cannot answer that honestly. The goal was built to cover everything in the backlog. Why Sprint Goals Lose Direction The Product Goal and Sprint Goal are supposed to cascade. The Scrum Guide says Sprints "enable predictability by ensuring inspection and adaptation of progress toward a Product Goal" [1]. Sprint Planning checks how selected items "map to the Product Goal" [1]. Each Sprint Goal is a planned step toward the Product Goal. Without a real Product Goal, Sprint Goals describe what will ship this Sprint. The connection to any larger direction gets lost. Teams commit to shipping features with no connection to where the product is supposed to end up. This shows up in Sprint Reviews: teams present what was built, stakeholders check things off, and nobody asks how the Sprint contributed to the Product Goal. The Scrum Guide Expansion Pack names this gap in the artifact itself [3]. Output done means the increment was built. Outcome done is the harder test: whether the business goal was reached. A team without a functioning Product Goal can only say whether the increment was built. The connection between Sprint Goal and Product Goal breaks down quietly. No single Sprint feels misaligned. Over time the product drifts, built sprint by sprint toward nowhere in particular. The Fulfill-or-Abandon Constraint The Scrum Guide requires the team to "fulfill (or abandon) one objective before taking on the next" [1], a constraint that rarely comes up in Sprint Planning. A specific Product Goal lets the team eventually confirm whether they reached it, or decided not to pursue it. A vague goal broad enough to cover the whole backlog can never be fulfilled, and without a clear destination, progress cannot be measured. It never gets inspected at a Sprint Review, because there is nothing concrete enough to check against. Writing a Product Goal commits the team to eventually answering whether the product did what they set out to do. Without that commitment, the team builds indefinitely and never decides whether they arrived. The harder case is the established product with no natural end point. A SaaS platform running for a decade cannot "fulfill" a goal like "be the most reliable tool in the market." That objection is fair, but narrowing the scope solves it: not "be the most reliable" but something measurable in a defined period. The Product Goal names the next destination. The fulfill-or-abandon language exists because the goal is supposed to be finite, not because every product has a built-in expiry date. Three Questions A Product Goal doing its job makes the backlog smaller. Items either advance toward it or they do not. The first question is the most important: can the Scrum Team use it to reject a backlog item? If the goal is specific enough to say no to something, it is filtering. If every item qualifies, the goal has no filtering function. Most teams, when pressed, cannot reject anything using theirs. Does the most recent Sprint Goal connect to it? items.title: We’re Not Paid to Practice Scrum, but Answer 5 Product Questions
items.summary: TL;DR: Five Product Questions Cheap Code Makes More Expensive to Skip For decades, the cost of building software rationed what an organization could start: nobody could afford to build everything, so somebody had to choose, however crudely. AI has weakened that rationing; the frontier labs need your organization to use more AI with every model generation, and the product operating model promises to fix what Agile supposedly broke. None of this guarantees that anyone asks whether the work solves a customer problem, nor whether solving it was worth the cost. You need to address these product questions yourself. These product questions become more expensive to skip when starting work gets cheap: which problem is worth solving, whether the work is the best use of the team’s time, whether it is good enough for the people who will see it, whether it solved the problem, and whether the team’s way of working still fits. AI agents can prepare evidence under the A3 Framework’s Assist category, where the agent analyzes and people decide, while explicit standards for AI-assisted work, such as the AI Definition of Done, and recurring inspections, such as the AI Delegation Audit, keep the answers honest. Whether you call any of this Scrum is the least interesting question of all. Image Thesis : This article explains five product questions that become more consequential when AI makes software implementation cheap, why falling AI costs increase the volume of work those questions must filter, and how teams set working principles during early AI adoption. Disclaimer : I read Charniak/McDermott’s book on “Artificial Intelligence” decades ago; of course, I use AI for research, translations, proofreading, challenging story arcs and article structures, creating artifacts such as graphics, and summarization. It is a production tool, not a substitute for thinking. If We’re Not Paid to Practice Scrum, What Are We Paid For? If you work in product, you probably believe that the slow, expensive build was the big problem of software development and that AI coding agents are finally solving it. Half of that belief holds up: building was slow and expensive, and agents have made writing code much cheaper. The other half deserves more scrutiny, because the expense was doing a crude rationing job that many organizations never replaced with anything better. When a feature took a team several weeks, somebody had to decide which idea got those weeks, and some weak ideas died in a prioritization meeting before anyone wrote a line of code. (Not many, admittedly; the ones with a senior sponsor and budget authority usually survived, and being chosen said nothing about whether an idea addressed a worthwhile problem.) The same expense also did damage, discouraging cheap experiments and pushing organizations to defend features they had already paid for in a prime example of submitting to the sunk cost fallacy. Product management has a name for the discipline that rationing never supplied on its own, and Uri Levine, the co-founder of Waze, put it into the title of his 2023 book, Fall in Love with the Problem, Not the Solution . When writing code costs next to nothing, falling in love with your own solution becomes affordable again. At the same time, testing whether customers care becomes cheaper than ever. For years, I have used one sentence to describe what agile practitioners are actually paid for: We are not paid to practice Scrum but to solve our customers’ problems within the given constraints while contributing to the organization’s sustainability. That sentence seems more useful now than ever, as Agile in general and Scrum in particular are under pressure from two sides at once. Two Promises of Speed, and What Adoption Does Not Guarantee The first pressure comes from the product operating model Marty Cagan popularized. He made the point plainly when I interviewed him in 2024: “To be blunt, a Scrum team is quite amateur compared to a professional product team,” as he put it in our interview on the product operating model and Scrum’s future . On paper, the model covers the questions this article is about. SVPG’s introduction to the product operating model states that “leaders in product management, technology, and design are responsible for deciding which problems to solve,” and it asks teams to find solutions that are valuable, usable, feasible, and viable. Adoption is a different matter. In my August 2026 survey of 48 practitioners , only 1 of the 26 respondents whose organizations had adopted the model or were moving toward it reported “a fundamental change in how build decisions are made.” Of the others, 9 described mostly relabeling, 9 a mix of real change and relabeling, and 7 said it was too early to tell. The respondents report on their organizations, though, and the survey did not verify 26 distinct organizations. Putting the model’s vocabulary on the slides seems to be easy, whereas changing who decides what to build, and on which…

items.title: Scientists discover hidden brain changes linked to common sleep disorders
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that sleep disorders are associated with structural changes in brain regions that control attention, decision-making, and emotions, potentially explaining why disrupted sleep can affect everyday thinking and behavior. The findings, drawn from 57 brain imaging studies, reveal both shared and disorder-specific patterns that could lead to more targeted treatments.

items.title: Scientists discover a hidden warning sign of cannabis addiction
items.summary: A study of more than 17,700 US adults found that people who use cannabis in multiple forms have dramatically higher rates of daily consumption and addiction symptoms than those who stick primarily to one method. Nearly 67% of those who used almost every form met criteria for cannabis use disorder, compared with just 15% of people who mainly consumed edibles.

items.title: Beyond the Dam of Knowledge Hoarding
items.summary: Picture a developer. Let's call him Chris. Chris has been with the company for twelve years. He knows the billing module better than anyone. When something breaks there, everyone calls him. Documentation? Barely any. Pair programming? Not really his thing. Chris isn't a bad guy. Chris has simply learned how to survive in organizations. If you know something nobody else knows, you're needed. If you're needed, you're safe. For decades, that worked, until AI arrived. It reads the billing module in seconds. It explains to anyone on the team what Chris spent twelve years learning. It finds the bug that used to require a call to Chris. To Chris, this feels like a break-in. As if someone forced open the door to his safe room. What do people do when they feel threatened? They build the walls higher. Chris avoids the AI tools. He finds reasons why they won't work on "his" code. He holds on to his knowledge even tighter. Research has a name for this pattern: knowledge hiding. And it shows that people who hide knowledge end up hurting their own creativity the most. For Scrum Masters, one finding matters most. This effect gets stronger in a performance-driven climate and weaker in a climate focused on learning, mastery and collaboration. So the team climate makes a difference. And shaping that climate is our job. The Scrum Guide describes Scrum Masters as true leaders who serve the Scrum Team and the wider organization. Your job is not to convince Chris. And certainly not to expose him. Your job is to create a space where the dam is no longer necessary. That takes qualities often dismissed as "soft." Empathy. Listening. Sensing what goes unsaid in the team. These qualities are now becoming the core of the role. Because behind hoarded knowledge there is almost always a question nobody asks out loud: What am I still needed for when my knowledge is no longer special? Here is what you can do. Name the fear without judging it. In the Sprint Retrospective, in a one-on-one. "I notice AI is making some of us uneasy. I feel it too." That sentence opens more doors than any tool training. Tell a new story about value. Chris was never valuable because he memorized code. He was valuable because he understands why the system was built this way. What problems it solves. Where the traps are. AI can't replace that judgment. It needs it. Make learning visible and small. No big rollout. One pairing slot per Sprint where Chris works on his module with AI, together with a junior colleague. He brings the why, the AI brings the how, the colleague brings the questions. Celebrate sharing, not knowing. Change what gets recognized. Not "Who solved the hardest problem?" but "Who made sure the team can now solve it on their own?" Lead by not knowing. Say it openly: "I'm learning this too." When you let yourself be seen learning, your team can do the same. That's the Scrum value of openness in action. Knowledge that is held back builds up. It gets heavy. Eventually it seeps away. Knowledge that flows carries the whole team. AI doesn't take Chris's place. It takes away the dam he had to hide behind. What remains is what he is truly needed for. Our job as Scrum Masters is to walk with him to get there. Not in front of him. Beside him. How do you see this in your teams? Is there a Chris on yours?

Their different chemical compositions suggest they may contain the remains of separate destroyed planets.

items.title: NASA’s Swift telescope falls to Earth after nearly 22 years in space
items.summary: After nearly 22 years of exploring the universe’s most violent explosions, NASA’s Swift Observatory has re-entered Earth’s atmosphere over Indonesia. Originally designed to last just two years, the pioneering space telescope transformed our understanding of black holes, exploding stars, and mysterious cosmic outbursts.

items.title: For decades, we were told to avoid full-fat dairy. New research says otherwise
items.summary: Full-fat dairy may not be the health villain it has long been portrayed as, according to a new study finding that three daily servings did not worsen weight, cholesterol, or insulin resistance over 12 weeks. Researchers also observed improvements in blood pressure and nutrient intake, raising questions about longstanding recommendations to choose low-fat dairy.

items.title: Dead stars could break one of physics' most famous limits
items.summary: A surprising new discovery suggests that some dead stars can grow far more massive than scientists once thought possible. Computer simulations show that powerful magnetic fields could allow white dwarfs to reach 2.4 times the mass of the Sun, dramatically exceeding a famous limit that has stood for decades. The findings could help explain unusually bright supernova explosions that have long puzzled astronomers.
